1.pericope_label: I will sing of the mercies of the Lord for ever... Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations

schools.summary: Delitzsch refuses the artifice that identifies the Judahite Ethan with the Levite of the same name, and links the psalm to its neighbour by their shared coincidences with Job. Ellicott limits what the opening will bear — the Hebrew for 'ever' 'implies indefiniteness' rather than eternity — prefers a continuous 'is for ever being built up', and reads the exordium as deliberate craft.

Calvin dates the psalm long after David's death from its own ending, and finds its occasion in the division of the kingdom, which made the holy oracle look 'deceptive and vain'. Gill takes the chosen as 'mystical David, the Messiah', not David literally understood.

Clarke sets the composition in the captivity, divides the psalm into two grand parts, and argues from history that the natural line cannot be meant, since 'none of his race has sat on the Jewish throne for more than two thousand years'. Wesley reads the opening praise as a precaution against seeming ungrateful.

Henry turns the psalm's own method into counsel — complaint gets ease, praise gets joy. Spurgeon grounds the constancy of praise in the constancy of its object: 'sense sings but now and then, but faith is an eternal songster.'

Augustine builds on the name Ethan, which 'means strong': 'no man in this world is strong, except in the hope of God's promises.' He presses the verb of building — some God destroys and does not rebuild, some he destroys and rebuilds.

positions.view: Long after David's death, over the division of the kingdom — a spectacle that made the promise look overthrown 'at the close of the life of one man'.
'It is most probable that this Psalm was composed during the captivity.'
Undetermined: only that 'the old Asaphic origin of the Psalm has been contested'.

debates.question: How long is the 'for ever' of the promise?

positions.view: Indefinite, not eternal: the Hebrew 'has properly neither the abstract idea of negation of time, nor the concrete (Christian) idea of eternity'.
Everlasting, and fulfilled in Christ, since the natural line failed and 'the Christ has reigned invariably since that time'.

outliers.view: The only voice to read the joyful opening as a literary device — the note of inviolability struck hard so that the later complaint of neglect should strike harder.

themes: I will sing of the mercies of the Lord for ever: with my mouth will I make known thy faithfulness to all generations.
For I have said, Mercy shall be built up for ever: thy faithfulness shalt thou establish in the very heavens.
I have made a covenant with my chosen, I have sworn unto David my servant,
Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations. Selah.

5.pericope_label: And the heavens shall praise thy wonders, O Lord... O Lord God of hosts, who is a strong Lord like unto thee?

schools.summary: Ellicott explains the turn from promise to praise as an appeal 'to nature and history', repunctuates the seventh verse into apposition with the sixth, and thinks the English limps where 'the Hebrew marches more grandly'. Delitzsch supplies the pressure: the house of David 'was threatened with assault from violent foes'.

Gill canvasses four senses of 'the heavens' before settling on the angels, and concedes every virtue to them while denying the comparison: they are 'holy, wise, knowing, powerful, faithful, kind, and merciful creatures, yet not to be compared with the Lord'.

Clarke turns the assembly into a rebuke — 'where this does not prevail, there is no true worship' — distinguishes scriptural boldness from a boldness 'reprehensible, if not sinful', and pictures the promises standing about the throne as an eastern monarch's servants. Wesley glosses the saints as 'the whole society of angels'.

Henry makes praise a duty owed by assemblies, the more the better since 'it is the more like heaven'. Spurgeon divides the labour between the choirs: those above praise the wonders of divine love, those below its faithfulness.

debates.question: Who is the 'congregation of the saints'?

positions.view: The hosts above — 'holy ones' being a standing term for angels.
The assemblies of the saints on earth, so that 'the whole family in heaven and earth' joins in the praise.

debates.question: What is the faithfulness that surrounds God?

positions.view: Either reading will do: 'we must either think of the attendant throngs of loyal angels, or of God clothed as it were with faithfulness'.
Attendants: the promises 'stand round his throne as the faithful servants of an eastern monarch stand round their master'.
A garment: faithfulness lies about God 'like a girdle encompassing thee'.

outliers.view: The only voice to turn the verse on the worshippers themselves, distinguishing a proper boldness at the throne of grace from one 'reprehensible, if not sinful'.

themes: And the heavens shall praise thy wonders, O Lord: thy faithfulness also in the congregation of the saints.
For who in the heaven can be compared unto the Lord? who among the sons of the mighty can be likened unto the Lord?
God is greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints, and to be had in reverence of all them that are about him.
O Lord God of hosts, who is a strong Lord like unto thee? or to thy faithfulness round about thee?

9.pericope_label: Thou rulest the raging of the sea... For the Lord is our defence; and the Holy One of Israel is our king

schools.summary: Ellicott traces the poet's associations from the sea to Egypt, corrects 'habitation' of the throne to 'foundation, or pillars', puts the verbs of the fifteenth verse into the present, and turns the closing verse round — 'of Jehovah is our shield' rather than 'the Lord is our defence'. His note on 'ornament' draws a national moral from a single word.
Gill sees God's power over the sea in his assigning it its place, hears the gospel in the joyful sound, and records the alternative rendering of the last verse while keeping the received sense.

Clarke argues the power from a storm at sea, offers 'Thou, like a hero, hast broken down Egypt', notes a line carried in one early printed Hebrew Bible that the received text lacks, and reads the joyful sound as the jubilee trumpet. Wesley takes Tabor and Hermon for the parts of Canaan and their rejoicing for fertility.
Spurgeon adds the plainest gloss on the joyful sound, that 'praise is a peculiarly joyful sound, and blessed are those who are familiar with its strains'.

debates.question: Why are Tabor and Hermon named?

positions.view: As a compass: with north and south, 'all the four quarters of the globe are intended'.
Partly for direction, but chiefly 'for their prominence and importance in the landscape' — and they 'sing for joy'.
As the parts of Canaan on either side of Jordan, their rejoicing being fertility: they 'shall be fruitful and prosperous'.
The jubilee trumpet, 'which proclaims deliverance to the captives'.
The shouting and music of the festivals — praise itself.
The gospel, or the ordinances to which the trumpets summoned.

outliers.view: The only voice to get a doctrine of national greatness out of the word 'ornament' — humility and acknowledgment of God, not triumphs or prosperity, being the crown of a nation's strength.

themes: Thou rulest the raging of the sea: when the waves thereof arise, thou stillest them.
Thou hast broken Rahab in pieces, as one that is slain; thou hast scattered thine enemies with thy strong arm.
The heavens are thine, the earth also is thine: as for the world and the fulness thereof, thou hast founded them.
The north and the south thou hast created them: Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in thy name.
Thou hast a mighty arm: strong is thy hand, and high is thy right hand.
Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne: mercy and truth shall go before thy face.
Blessed is the people that know the joyful sound: they shall walk, O Lord, in the light of thy countenance.
In thy name shall they rejoice all the day: and in thy righteousness shall they be exalted.
For thou art the glory of their strength: and in thy favour our horn shall be exalted.
For the Lord is our defence; and the Holy One of Israel is our king.

19.pericope_label: Then thou spakest in vision to thy holy one... my faithfulness and my mercy shall be with him: and in my name shall his horn be exalted

schools.summary: Ellicott concedes the manuscript evidence for the plural and rejects it, identifies the speaker as Nathan, describes the oracle's form and its source, and notices that faithfulness and mercy, God's own attendants earlier in the psalm, are here 'commissioned to act as a guard to David and his house'.

Gill turns the preposition, rendering 'concerning thy Holy One' so that the Messiah is the subject rather than the hearer, and distinguishes the strict justice shown to Christ as surety from the mercy that is with him as Mediator.

Clarke reports that well over a hundred manuscripts and all the versions read the plural, and defends the literal promise from the record, since David 'was never overthrown' and every revolt only seated him more firmly. Wesley reads the singular as a plural, 'especially to Samuel and Nathan'.

Henry notes that David was chosen 'not out of the princes, but the shepherds', and that swearing by holiness is swearing by God himself. Spurgeon draws the practical conclusion: 'let us lay our faith where God has laid our help.'

debates.question: Who is the 'holy one' spoken to?

positions.view: Read plurally with the versions: Samuel, Nathan and Gad — or at least Samuel and Nathan.
Nathan. 'The singular is correct', and it was to him that the word came by night.
Neither: read 'concerning thy Holy One', making the Messiah the subject of the vision rather than its hearer.

debates.question: What can the enemy not do to him?

positions.view: Not 'exact' but perhaps 'surprise him', or on a third reading 'lead him astray' — the received sense being only one of several.
Not 'conquer him or make him tributary' — and for Gill, not deceive him either.

outliers.view: The only voice to test the promise of invincibility against David's actual campaigns, listing the revolts and coalitions that failed and concluding he 'was never overthrown'.

themes: Then thou spakest in vision to thy holy one, and saidst, I have laid help upon one that is mighty; I have exalted one chosen out of the people.
I have found David my servant; with my holy oil have I anointed him:
With whom my hand shall be established: mine arm also shall strengthen him.
The enemy shall not exact upon him; nor the son of wickedness afflict him.
And I will beat down his foes before his face, and plague them that hate him.
But my faithfulness and my mercy shall be with him: and in my name shall his horn be exalted.

25.pericope_label: I will set his hand also in the sea... It shall be established for ever as the moon, and as a faithful witness in heaven

schools.summary: Ellicott dates the psalm from the word 'Father', 'a title for the Divine Being which the national religion did not frame till the exile period', bounds the promised dominion to the Solomonic limits, gets the paradox out of the firstborn title, and repoints the last verse so that the faithful witness in heaven is the moon. Delitzsch reads the dominion as world-wide instead, though 'indefinite and universal'.

Gill fixes which fatherhood is meant — 'not by creation... nor by adoption... but by generation' — denies the enduring seed of the natural line, and treats the divine oath as accommodation to human weakness.

Clarke fulfils the dominion historically in David's conquests, loosens 'first-born' to mean a best-beloved son, argues that the promise 'can apply only to the spiritual David', and makes the single oath sufficient, since 'there needs no second oath'. Wesley reads the sea and rivers as the bounds of the promised land and takes the faithful witness for the rainbow.

debates.question: How far does the promised dominion reach?

positions.view: To the bounds of the Solomonic kingdom — the Mediterranean and the Euphrates, 'the uttermost bounds of the promised land'.
World-wide, 'not merely dominion within the compass promised in the primeval times', though the language here is indefinite.
As far as it actually went: David's empire along the coast, with the further shores paying tribute.

debates.question: What is the faithful witness in heaven?

positions.view: The moon — arbiter of the festivals that were signs of the covenant, and the measure by which time itself is kept.
The rainbow, 'a token of God's everlasting covenant between God and every living creature'.

outliers.view: The only voice to date the psalm from the theological history of a single title, arguing that Israel did not call God Father until the exile.

themes: I will set his hand also in the sea, and his right hand in the rivers.
He shall cry unto me, Thou art my father, my God, and the rock of my salvation.
Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth.
My mercy will I keep for him for evermore, and my covenant shall stand fast with him.
His seed also will I make to endure for ever, and his throne as the days of heaven.
If his children forsake my law, and walk not in my judgments;
If they break my statutes, and keep not my commandments;
Then will I visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes.
Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail.
My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips.
Once have I sworn by my holiness that I will not lie unto David.
His seed shall endure for ever, and his throne as the sun before me.
It shall be established for ever as the moon, and as a faithful witness in heaven. Selah.

38.pericope_label: But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed... thou hast covered him with shame

schools.summary: Ellicott insists the expostulation must not be softened — 'the point of the poem, indeed, is gone if we soften down these expressions' — and argues that the blunted sword preserves a memory of the stone age, the word for edge being 'rock', in a case 'where the condition of modern science helps us in exegesis of the Bible'.
Gill applies the broken hedges to the church rather than the land, its members made havoc of and its ministers scattered.

Clarke puts the contradiction as a question — 'God cannot lie to David; how is it then that his crown is profaned?' — traces the spoiling through Chaldeans, Assyrians, Samaritans and Idumeans, illustrates the failed weapon from metallurgy, and counts the short reigns of the last kings. Wesley makes the shortened youth dynastic rather than personal.

Henry admits the difficulty of reconciling providences with promises while denying that rebukes repeal a covenant, and offers two datings on either of which the complaint holds. Spurgeon grants the liberty to expostulate, since 'this holy and inspired man did so unrebuked'.

debates.question: Is the blunted sword an edge or a flint?

positions.view: A flint. The Hebrew is 'rock', and 'the word flint for the edge of a weapon might easily survive the actual use of the implement itself' — the ancient versions, knowing nothing of the stone age, paraphrased it away.
An edge, turned or broken — illustrated from soldiers whose swords bend at every blow for want of hardened iron.
The last kings of Judah, none of whom 'reigned half their days'.
The kingdom's: its flourishing estate 'reached not beyond his next successor'.
Christ's, who 'did not live out half the time of man's age'.

outliers.view: The only voice to defend the boldness of the expostulation as essential rather than embarrassing, holding that conviction of the promise is what licenses the vehemence of the complaint.

themes: But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed.
Thou hast made void the covenant of thy servant: thou hast profaned his crown by casting it to the ground.
Thou hast broken down all his hedges; thou hast brought his strong holds to ruin.
All that pass by the way spoil him: he is a reproach to his neighbours.
Thou hast set up the right hand of his adversaries; thou hast made all his enemies to rejoice.
Thou hast also turned the edge of his sword, and hast not made him to stand in the battle.
Thou hast made his glory to cease, and cast his throne down to the ground.
The days of his youth hast thou shortened: thou hast covered him with shame. Selah.

46.pericope_label: How long, Lord? wilt thou hide thyself for ever?... Blessed be the Lord for evermore. Amen, and Amen

schools.summary: Ellicott hears in the cry a faith that 'is not extinct, though it has a sore struggle with despair', treats one clause as damaged — as it stands it 'might possibly be an incoherent sob' — sharpens 'what man' to 'what hero, or champion', and reports the rabbinic reading that refers the reproach to the Messiah's delay.

Gill takes the hidden face as of the same kind with an eternal absence, and denies that the closing blessing is a copyist's, holding it the psalmist's own, uttered when he saw the complaint reconciled to the covenant.

Clarke asks the psalm's question in his own voice, quotes at length a paraphrase that makes the reproach fall on the slowness of the Messiah's coming, and argues from manuscripts that the closing doxology 'has been added by a later hand' to divide the books of the Psalter. Wesley holds both readings of the anointed's footsteps open, and blesses God while the complaint still stands.

positions.view: Israel's whole history: 'every step taken by Israel was the subject of reproach', traced up to the earliest times to prove them rebellious.
Or the Messiah's delay: the enemies 'have reproached the slowness of the footsteps of the feet of thy Messiah', mocking an expectation that never arrives.
A later hand. It marks the end of the Third Book, is missing or set apart in several manuscripts, though 'it is found in all the ancient Versions'.
The psalmist himself — 'not the words of the copier of the Psalms, blessing God for assistance in prosecuting the work thus far'.

outliers.view: The only voice to entertain the text as it stands as an inarticulate cry — 'an incoherent sob' — before preferring the emendation that regularises it.

themes: How long, Lord? wilt thou hide thyself for ever? shall thy wrath burn like fire?
Remember how short my time is: wherefore hast thou made all men in vain?
What man is he that liveth, and shall not see death? shall he deliver his soul from the hand of the grave? Selah.
Lord, where are thy former lovingkindnesses, which thou swarest unto David in thy truth?
Remember, Lord, the reproach of thy servants; how I do bear in my bosom the reproach of all the mighty people;
Wherewith thine enemies have reproached, O Lord; wherewith they have reproached the footsteps of thine anointed.
Blessed be the Lord for evermore. Amen, and Amen.
